title: Hot weather, hotter opinions on first day of in-person early voting
summary: Some were tired of the barrage of campaign ads. Some heard those ads, because they brought the campaigns' messages with them, and others came to their decision the old-fashioned way -- the personal touch. They all showed up for the first day of early voting.
content:
by William J. Ford and Mayah Nachman, Maryland Matters June 12, 2026

by William J. Ford and Mayah Nachman, Maryland Matters June 12, 2026

Some were tired of the constant barrage of campaign ads. Some had apparently listened to those ads, because they brought the campaigns’ messages with them to the voting centers. And some, like Patty McGuire of Bowie, came to their decision the old-fashioned way — the personal touch.

“My son went to high school with him and had nice things to say about him,” McGuire said of her vote for Del. Adrian Boafo (D-Prince George’s), one of more than two dozen Democrats seeking the nomination to run for the congressional seat held for more than 40 years by Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-5th), who is not running for reelection.

Mail-in ballots have been available for weeks to voters who requested them but for others, Thursday marked the first day of early voting for the primary election set for June 23. Early voting will continue through next Thursday.

At early voting centers around the state, dozens of volunteers and candidates sporting campaign paraphernalia turned out in unseasonably humid weather for the few voters who were on hand early. At Bowie City Gymnasium in Prince George’s County, only five people stood in line as the polls opened at 7 a.m.

Gina Moore was first in line at the center where voters weighed the race for Hoyer’s seat — along with party nominations for statewide office, legislative seats, county and local officials, as voters primary voters around the state are deciding. In Maryland, which has a closed primary system, only voters affiliated with Republican or Democratic parties vote in the primary, to choose their nominees for the November general election.

In the race for 5th District – which includes parts of Prince George’s and Anne Arundel counties and all of Charles, Calvert and St. Mary’s counties – Moore said she was voting for Quincy Bareebe, the CEO of a home health business, over Boafo, who had the personal endorsement of Hoyer.

“I chose Quincy because I did not like what I heard about Adrian. He’s a lobbyist,” said Moore, a retired federal employee.

In upper Montgomery County, where voters were choosing their nominees for the 6th District, people said they heard a lot about the two front-running Democratic candidates — too much, in fact.

“Here I am, ready to vote and I’m still a little up in the air because … it bothers me that both of them just call each other a liar. It’s like, who do you believe?” said Krista Abbaticchio, a lifelong Montgomery County resident, outside the polling place at the Germantown Community Recreation Center.

Abbaticchio was talking about Rep. April McClain Delaney (D-6th) and former Rep. David Trone. The two Democrats have poured millions into the race — in Trone’s case, much of it his own money — attacking the other and each claiming to be the best candidate to confront President Donald Trump and his policies.

While some voters declined to say whom they chose, they all expressed frustration about the ads in the 6th District.

“I feel like many people, that essentially I don’t think Congress has accomplished much of anything,” said Marian Lesko, at the polls at the Damascus Community Recreation Center. “I’m really hoping [her candidate] a better chance of accomplishing something.”

Montgomery County resident Courtney Low said she “hates” how much money the two have spent to fund their campaigns.

“It’s just among the wasted dollars there’s been in these campaigning ads and nonstop phone calls and text messages and people coming to our door and everyday we get mailers,” she said. “I’m just disgusted by the amount of money they’ve spent on this election.”

Low, who voted at the Germantown voting center, chose McClain Delaney due to endorsements she got from major Democrats, such as Gov. Wes Moore, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-8th).

“I support them and I think they know better than I do what matters for our district,” Low said. “I don’t know every single thing that is going on, but I believe they do, as it’s their job, and I trust their opinion.”

Back in the 5th District, ads made the difference for Charles Milling, 18, voting for the first time. He came to the voting center at Bowie with his mom, Trina, to vote for Boafo, 32.

“I saw him on ads on TV and YouTube. I thought he was a good candidate, someone who can stand up to all the other harsher Republicans and candidates out there like Trump,” said Charles Milling, who attends at Hampton University in Hampton, Virginia.

“I think he’s someone who could mentor the youth, too,” he said. “Because of his age, he’s more understanding of where we’re coming from in this generation.”

Outside the voting center, music blared through speakers in the parking lot where dozens of volunteers stood outside anxiously waiting to talk with any voter headed toward the gymnasium.

Several Democratic candidates for the 5th District visited Bowie early Thursday morning including Bareebe, Boafo, former Prince George’s County Executive Rushern L. Baker III and Walter Kirkland, a business and marketing consultant and founder of 100 Black Men of Prince George’s County.

The smiles, hugs and picture-taking were amplified when Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) stopped in support of Boafo as well as her longtime colleague and friend Tara Jackson, who’s seeking the Democratic nomination to remain Prince George’s County state’s attorney.

Further south in the district, in Charles County, there was no music, but still the stifling heat and the scarcity of voters.

Gaylord Hogue said he voted for fellow Democrat and Charles County resident Sen. Arthur Ellis in the crowded 5th District race.

One main reason Hogue chose Ellis is the continued push to get rapid transit in the county. Another reason is how Ellis “was fighting” to demand the chamber vote on a redistricting bill to redraw the state’s eight congressional districts.

“I think he really showed himself well,” Hogue said. “I just don’t think the heads of the state of Maryland [endorsed] the right person.”

Early voting runs until June 18 and Election Day on June 23. Polls open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. For more information, check out our voter guide.
